newsitem.title: USA: US funding for development banks "do-able" - Rubin.
newsitem.headline: US funding for development banks "do-able" - Rubin.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Friday it would be "difficult but do-able" for the administration to convince Congress to fully fund U.S. contributions to the multilateral development banks.

"We must maintain U.S. leadership by meeting our financial commitments to these institutions," he told the Bretton Woods Committee, a group which promotes U.S. participation in the international financial institutions.
Noting that the United States was the only nation behind on its payments to the World Bank, Rubin said, "That must not be allowed to continue."

The current Republican-led Congress approved $700 million of funding for the World Bank's International Development Association (IDA) affiliate, leaving America $234.5 million in arrears to IDA, which lends money to very poor nations.
"If past is prologue, it is going to very difficult --- difficult but do-able" to obtain the financing, Rubin said.

Because of the difficulty that the United States has had in meeting its commitments to IDA, the affiliate is being partly financed in 1996/97 by an Interim Trust Fund drawn from other donor nations. U.S. companies have been barred from bidding on contracts financed by the Trust Fund.
Some U.S. lawmakers have criticized the Bank for those procurement restrictions and have threatened to withhold future IDA funding in response.
The Treasury for its part has called the restrictions counter-productive for the continued survival of IDA and has urged other nations to lift them.

Rubin told reporters after his speech that the United States faced a tough task in convincing other countries of its case. "It's very much an uphill battle and I can't predict where it will come out,' he said.
In his remarks to the Bretton Woods Committee, Rubin warned that IDA would "suffer terribly" if the United States did not provide its promised contributions.
"I do very much fear that other nations will start to pull away from IDA and they'll go into a bilateral mode and IDA will suffer terribly," he said, "That would be a tragedy."
Rubin also told reporters that the Clinton administration would continue to press Congress for funding for the Middle East development bank, despite opposition from some lawmakers.
